problems.title: Minimum Positive Sum Subarray
problems.problem: Given an integer array nums and two integers l and r, look at every subarray whose length is between l and r (inclusive). Among those whose sum is strictly greater than 0, return the smallest sum. If none exist, return -1.

examples.explanation: Valid positive subarrays are [3,-2]=1, [1,4]=5, [3,-2,1]=2, [-2,1,4]=3. The smallest is 1.
No subarray of length 2 or 3 has a sum greater than 0, so the answer is -1.
[1,2] has length 2 and sum 3, which is the smallest positive sum possible.

problems.intuition: n is at most 100, so we can afford to look at every subarray. Fix a start index i and extend the end j one step at a time while keeping a running sum, so each new subarray costs O(1) instead of re-adding all its elements. Only lengths from l to r count, and only positive sums are candidates.
approach: Set ans = Integer.MAX_VALUE.
For each start i, reset sum = 0.
Move j from i forward while the length j - i + 1 is at most r, adding nums.get(j) to sum.
If the length is at least l and sum > 0, set ans = min(ans, sum).
After all starts, return -1 if ans was never updated, else ans.
dryRun: i=0: j=0 sum=3 (len 1, too short); j=1 sum=1 (len 2, positive) ans=1; j=2 sum=2 (len 3) ans stays 1; j=3 would be len 4 > r, stop
i=1: j=1 sum=-2; j=2 sum=-1 (not positive); j=3 sum=3 (len 3) ans=min(1,3)=1
i=2: j=2 sum=1 (len 1, too short); j=3 sum=5 (len 2) ans stays 1

complexity.time: O(n * r), at most O(n^2) = 10^4 steps for n = 100

edgeCases: All sums zero or negative: ans stays MAX, return -1
l = r: only one window size is checked
Single element with l = r = 1: return it if positive, else -1
Zero sums do not count because the sum must be strictly greater than 0
problems.takeaway: When n is small, fix the start and grow the end with a running sum to check every subarray in O(n^2) without an extra loop for the sum.

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.problem: Given the root of a binary tree, mirror it: swap the left and right child of every node. Return the root.

examples.explanation: Every node's children are swapped, so the tree becomes its mirror image.
The root's two children 1 and 3 swap places.

problems.intuition: A tree is mirrored if both of its subtrees are mirrored and then placed on the opposite sides. That is a natural recursion: solve the left and right subtrees, then swap them at the current node.
approach: If root is null, return null.
Recursively invert the left subtree and save it in l.
Set root.left to the inverted right subtree.
Set root.right to l.
Return root.
dryRun: invertTree(2): l = invertTree(1) = 1 (leaf, children null), root.left = invertTree(3) = 3, root.right = 1, so 2 now has children 3, 1
root.left = invertTree(7): inside, l = 6, root.left = 9, root.right = 6, so 7 now has children 9, 6

complexity.time: O(n), each node is visited once
complexity.space: O(h) recursion stack, h = height (O(n) worst case for a skewed tree)

edgeCases: Empty tree: return null
Single node: nothing to swap
Skewed tree (only left children) becomes only right children
Duplicate values do not matter, we swap pointers not values
problems.takeaway: Many tree problems are just 'solve left, solve right, combine at the root'. Save one child in a temp variable before overwriting it.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k values that appear most often. Any order is fine, and the answer is guaranteed to be unique.

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times and 2 appears 2 times, more than 3 which appears once.
Only one distinct value, so it is the answer.
1 and 2 appear 4 times each, 3 appears twice.

problems.intuition: A frequency can never be more than n. So instead of sorting values by frequency (O(n log n)), drop each value into bucket number f where f is its count. Then walk the buckets from the highest frequency down and pick values until we have k. This is bucket sort and runs in O(n).
approach: Count every value in a HashMap cnt.
Make an array of lists b of size n + 1; b[f] holds values that appear exactly f times.
For each key x, add it to b[cnt.get(x)].
Walk f from n down to 1, copying values from b[f] into res until idx reaches k.
Return res.
dryRun: f = 2: res[1] = 2, idx = 2, loop condition idx < k fails

complexity.time: O(n) for counting and walking the buckets
complexity.space: O(n) for the map and buckets

edgeCases: k equals the number of distinct values: return all of them
All elements equal: one bucket at f = n
Negative numbers work since the map keys are values, not indexes
Several values in one bucket: the inner break stops exactly at k
problems.takeaway: When the key you sort by is bounded by n (like a count), bucket it by that key to beat O(n log n). A min-heap of size k is the other common answer.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.problem: You get an m x n grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water). Land cells that touch up, down, left or right form one island. Count the islands.

examples.explanation: All the land cells are connected, so there is one island.
A 2x2 block at the top left, a single cell in the middle and a pair at the bottom right.

problems.intuition: Each time we find a land cell that has not been visited, we have found a new island. Flood fill from it (BFS) to mark every connected land cell as water, so the same island is never counted again. BFS with a queue is used instead of recursion because a 300 x 300 grid of all land would make recursive DFS go about 90000 calls deep and risk a stack overflow.
approach: Set cnt = 0 and dirs = the four moves.
Scan every cell (i, j). Skip it if it is not '1'.
Found new land: cnt++, set grid[i][j] = '0' and push it into q.
While q is not empty: poll cur, try all 4 neighbours (x, y); if inside the grid and '1', set it to '0' and push it.
When the scan ends, return cnt.
dryRun: q is empty, all 9 land cells are now '0'
the rest of the scan only sees '0', so return cnt = 1

complexity.time: O(m * n), each cell is pushed at most once
complexity.space: O(min(m, n)) for the BFS queue in practice, O(m * n) worst case

edgeCases: All water: return 0
All land: one island
Checkerboard: every land cell is its own island (diagonals do not connect)
1 x 1 grid
Note: the grid is modified in place; copy it first if the caller needs it
problems.takeaway: Counting connected components on a grid = scan + flood fill (BFS, DFS or Union-Find). Mark cells visited when you push them, not when you pop them, to avoid duplicates in the queue.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.problem: Given strings s and t, find the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t, counting duplicates. Return "" if there is no such substring.

examples.explanation: BANC contains A, B and C and no shorter window does.
The whole string is the minimum window.
t needs two 'a's but s has only one, so no window works.

problems.intuition: Use a sliding window [l, r]. cnt[c] stores how many more copies of c the window still needs (it goes negative for extra copies). need counts the total characters of t still missing. Grow r until need hits 0, meaning the window is valid; then shrink l as far as possible while it stays valid, recording the best length. Each index enters and leaves the window once, so it is O(m + n).
approach: cnt[c]++ for every c in t; need = t.length(), l = 0, start = 0, min = MAX.
For each r: if cnt[s[r]] > 0 before decrementing, this char was needed, so need--. Then cnt[s[r]]--.
While need == 0: if r - l + 1 < min, save min and start = l.
Then remove s[l]: cnt[s[l]]++; if it becomes > 0, the window is now missing it, so need++. Move l forward.
Return "" if min is still MAX, else s.substring(start, start + min).
dryRun: s = ADOBECODEBANC, t = ABC: cnt[A]=cnt[B]=cnt[C]=1, need = 3
r=0 A: needed, need = 2; r=1 D, r=2 O: extras, cnt goes to -1; r=3 B: need = 1; r=4 E: extra
r=5 C: need = 0. Window ADOBEC (len 6): min = 6, start = 0. Remove A: cnt[A] = 1 > 0, need = 1, l = 1
r=6 O, r=7 D, r=8 E: extras; r=9 B: cnt[B] was 0, extra, becomes -1
r=10 A: need = 0. Window l=1..10 len 10, not better. Shrink: remove D, O, B (cnt[B] back to 0), E, l = 5; len 6 not better; remove C: cnt[C] = 1, need = 1, l = 6
r=11 N: extra; r=12 C: need = 0. Window l=6..12 len 7, not better. Remove O, l = 7; len 6 not better; remove D, l = 8
len 5 < 6: min = 5, start = 8. Remove E, l = 9; len 4 < 5: min = 4, start = 9. Remove B: cnt[B] = 1, need = 1, l = 10, stop

complexity.time: O(m + n), l and r each move at most m times

edgeCases: t longer than s: need never reaches 0, return ""
t has duplicates like "aa": cnt handles counts, not just presence
Upper and lower case are different characters
Answer at the very end of a long string, e.g. 100000 x's followed by "yz"
problems.takeaway: Variable sliding window: expand right until valid, then shrink left while still valid and record the answer. A single 'need' counter avoids comparing two whole frequency maps each step.
